video_title: The West’s Forgotten War and the New Russia | Mark Galeotti
gist: Russia analyst Mark Galeotti argues the Ukraine war has split into three parallel conflicts (grinding attrition in the Donbas, economic deep-strikes, and a political battle for Western resolve), describes Vladimir Putin as a rational but insecurity-driven survivalist propped up by a small, financially dependent inner circle, and says Washington currently has no real Russia strategy beyond outsourcing the war's costs to a fracturing Europe.

themes.theme: The War as Three Parallel Conflicts

insights.claim: Mark Galeotti frames the Russia-Ukraine war as three simultaneous wars rather than one: a grinding kinetic battle of attrition in the Donbas, an economic war of deep strikes on Russian refineries and infrastructure, and a political/propaganda war fought inside Russian society and among Western allies.
insights.speaker: Mark Galeotti
insights.so_what: Investors tracking the war should separate battlefield, economic-strike, and political-will signals rather than reading them as one composite indicator of where the conflict is heading.
insights.quote: we could almost think of it as multiple wars or at least multiple fronts.

insights.claim: Russian forces are grinding forward toward control of the remaining part of the Donetsk region but advancing only slowly and at high human cost, and Galeotti warns against linearly extrapolating recent advance rates to forecast future territorial gains since conditions can shift quickly.
insights.speaker: Mark Galeotti
insights.so_what: Simple distance-per-week extrapolations of the front line are an unreliable way to time a battlefield-driven settlement or ceasefire.
insights.quote: there's a danger in trying to map too much onto sort of assessments of well they advanced 200 m in this period

insights.claim: Putin's territorial objective is not fixed at a predetermined line such as full control of Donetsk — Galeotti believes Putin will opportunistically expand his goals if battlefield conditions allow.
insights.speaker: Mark Galeotti
insights.so_what: Any negotiated settlement should be judged against a moving target, not a fixed Russian demand, since Putin's ask can grow with battlefield momentum.
insights.quote: I suspect Putin basically will go for whatever he thinks he can get.

insights.claim: Ukraine's deep-strike campaign has shifted beyond Russian ports and oil refineries to hit consumer-facing economic targets like Wildberries (rendered "Wildberries" in the transcript), the dominant Russian e-commerce platform dubbed the "Russian Amazon," explicitly to make ordinary Russians feel the war's economic cost.
insights.speaker: Mark Galeotti
insights.so_what: Signals a widening target set for Ukraine's strike campaign toward Russian domestic consumer/logistics infrastructure, relevant to anyone tracking Russian corporate or e-commerce risk.
insights.quote: Wildberries which is often quite rightly I think described as as the Russian Amazon

insights.claim: Every ruble the Russian state spends compensating victims of Ukraine's deep strikes on infrastructure is a ruble it cannot spend on producing tanks and missiles, making the strike campaign a direct fiscal trade-off against Russia's war-fighting capacity, not merely a symbolic gesture.
insights.speaker: Mark Galeotti
insights.so_what: Deep-strike campaigns should be read as a fiscal-pressure lever on Russian war production capacity, not just a morale operation.
insights.quote: every ruble that they might end up having to spend, for example, in compensating the people who are hit by the Wilders attacks is a ruble they can't spend on producing tanks and missiles.

insights.claim: Russia is expected to renew large-scale attacks on Ukraine's energy infrastructure through the coming winter and is increasingly targeting water treatment plants specifically, because cutting off both electricity and clean water simultaneously is a more effective way to make Ukrainian cities unlivable than targeting either alone.
insights.speaker: Mark Galeotti
insights.so_what: A harsher winter energy/water campaign is a likely near-term catalyst for renewed refugee outflows and Western aid pressure through Q1.
insights.quote: if you can cut off electricity and clean water, you begin to make Ukraine cities unlivable.

insights.claim: Total Russian casualties in the Ukraine war may be as high as 1.5 million, with roughly 500,000 or more killed and the remainder wounded seriously enough to be hospitalized or sent home rather than returned to combat, though Galeotti stresses there is no reliable methodology behind the number.
insights.speaker: Mark Galeotti
insights.so_what: Casualty attrition at this scale is a multi-year drag on Russian labor supply and a variable worth tracking against any ceasefire or negotiation timeline.
insights.quote: the overall casualty figure is anything up to about 1.5 million.

insights.claim: Russia's Ukraine-war losses (500,000+ dead) dwarf the roughly 60,000 American deaths across the entire Vietnam War, illustrating a societal casualty tolerance in today's Russia unusual by modern Western standards.
insights.speaker: Mark Galeotti
insights.so_what: Historical casualty-tolerance comparisons suggest Western assumptions about when domestic political pressure forces a ceasefire may not apply to Russia.
insights.quote: the Vietnam War produced less than 60,000 dead Americans.

insights.claim: Russian war casualties are drawn disproportionately from the poorest, least politically significant regions -- Dagistan in the north Caucasus and Bashiria in the east -- rather than Moscow, because Putin has avoided mass conscription and instead relies on volunteers lured by cash payments described as multiples of the average salary plus large death payouts to families.
insights.speaker: Mark Galeotti
insights.so_what: The war's human cost is politically insulated from Russia's power centers, helping explain the regime's capacity to sustain the conflict without domestic blowback in Moscow -- a key input for duration forecasts.
insights.quote: if you go to the impoverished regions, Dagistan in the north caucuses, Bashiria in the east and so forth, there you know, you can find villages which are basically being

insights.claim: Russian volunteer-soldier recruitment was running behind the pace of casualties earlier in the year and has only "perked up a little" since, functioning as a leading indicator of manpower strain on Russia's capacity to sustain offensive operations.
insights.speaker: Mark Galeotti
insights.so_what: Recruitment-versus-casualty trendlines are a useful proxy for how much longer Russia can sustain current offensive tempo without resorting to unpopular conscription.
insights.quote: certainly earlier this year actually we could see recruitment was lagging behind the casualty rate.

insights.claim: The mean age of soldiers fighting on both the Russian and Ukrainian sides is around 40, making this a war fought predominantly by middle-aged men rather than youth, partly because Putin has avoided the political risk of sending young conscripts into combat.
insights.speaker: Mark Galeotti
insights.so_what: Both economies are losing prime-working-age male labor rather than youth, compounding pre-existing demographic and productivity headwinds on both sides.
insights.quote: you have a mean age of of the the Russian soldiers and indeed Ukrainian soldiers which is around 40 years old.

insights.claim: Ukraine's actual casualty and conscription figures remain essentially unknown; even Western analysts sympathetic to Ukraine do not consider the figures occasionally released by President Zelensky to be credible.
insights.speaker: Mark Galeotti
insights.so_what: Public casualty figures from Kyiv should be treated as messaging rather than reliable data when modeling Ukraine's manpower runway.
insights.quote: even the more Ukraine sympathetic analysts I have spoken to within UK and other governments do not regard those figures as credible

insights.claim: Ukraine may actually be suffering a higher casualty rate than Russia relative to its shrinking remaining population, because millions of refugees -- mainly women and children -- have fled to Europe, concentrating combat risk on a smaller pool of remaining Ukrainian men.
insights.speaker: Mark Galeotti
insights.so_what: Proportional casualty burden, not absolute numbers, is the more relevant metric for gauging how much longer Ukraine's manpower base can sustain the war.

insights.claim: Ukraine has increasingly moved toward a forced-conscription model nicknamed "busification," in which officers from local military commissariats grab men off the street and load them onto buses, sometimes prompting crowds to intervene -- visible in videos circulating online.
insights.speaker: Mark Galeotti
insights.so_what: Coercive recruitment signals Ukraine's voluntary manpower pool is strained, raising the strategic importance of drone/autonomous-systems substitution for infantry.
insights.quote: officers from the local mil military commisseriat will stop people on the streets, grab them, throw them into buses and drive them off.

insights.claim: Russia's already below-replacement fertility rate compounds the demographic damage from war attrition, creating long-term labor-force consequences that are not currently priced into most assessments of Russian national power.
insights.speaker: Mark Galeotti
insights.so_what: Long-horizon Russia risk models should weight demographic decline plus war attrition together, not treat the war as a temporary, reversible shock.

insights.claim: US military assistance to Ukraine has shifted from direct provision of American equipment to a system (called the "pearl system" in the transcript) in which European countries pay to purchase US-made kit on Ukraine's behalf, while US intelligence-sharing and targeting packages -- described as central to Ukraine's long-range strikes into Russia -- continue uninterrupted.
insights.speaker: Mark Galeotti
insights.so_what: Ukraine's ability to sustain deep strikes still depends on continued US intelligence-sharing even as direct hardware aid winds down -- a single lever Washington retains to pressure either side.
insights.quote: it is still providing intelligence and that is absolutely crucial targeting packages which are central to the Ukrainian longrange strikes deep into Russia.

insights.claim: The US has deprioritized Ukraine's access to Patriot interceptor missiles because Washington is focused on restocking its own and its Gulf allies' magazines after both fired large numbers of interceptors during the Gulf conflict, showing how a competing US military theater directly crowds out supply available to Ukraine.
insights.speaker: Mark Galeotti
insights.so_what: Air-defense interceptor availability for Ukraine is now a function of Gulf theater demand, not just Ukraine-specific policy -- a hidden cross-theater supply constraint to watch.
insights.quote: now the priority is for the United states to restock its magazines because of the Gulf War, but also its Gulf allies who have been shooting off vast numbers of these interceptors

insights.claim: NATO members have agreed to a defense-spending target of roughly 3.5% of GDP, but European governments are simultaneously trying to rearm their own militaries and supply Ukraine, and Galeotti believes domestic rearmament is winning that internal budget competition.
insights.speaker: Mark Galeotti
insights.so_what: Rising European defense budgets may not translate proportionally into more Ukraine aid, since domestic rearmament is claiming priority within the same spending envelope.

insights.claim: European military aid to Ukraine varies sharply by geography and threat perception: Scandinavian and Baltic states, which view Russia as the direct existential threat, have given disproportionately more aid, while Mediterranean states such as Spain, Italy, and Greece have been notably less generous because they see the Middle East/North Africa region as their primary security concern.
insights.speaker: Mark Galeotti
insights.so_what: Intra-European burden-sharing is structurally uneven and unlikely to converge, since it reflects genuinely different national threat assessments rather than mere stinginess.
insights.quote: If you are Spain or Italy or indeed Greece, actually you see the real threat as coming from the Middle East, North African region

insights.claim: Britain has handed over almost all of its self-propelled artillery to Ukraine, an example of European militaries depleting their own equipment stocks to a degree that is starting to make some governments uncomfortable about their own residual capability.
insights.speaker: Mark Galeotti
insights.so_what: Defense-industrial replenishment for depleted European stocks (artillery, armor) is a multi-year procurement tailwind for European and allied defense manufacturers.
insights.quote: Britain basically for example handed over almost all it self-rebelled artillery

insights.claim: Political churn expected across France, Germany, and the UK over the next roughly 12 months could weaken Western support for Ukraine: French President Macron is embattled ahead of elections with a possible government led by the explicitly Ukraine-skeptic Le Pen; German Chancellor Merz is similarly embattled amid the rise of the anti-Ukraine-support AFD movement; and the UK's new prime minister faces competing domestic fiscal priorities such as social care that could squeeze the defense/Ukraine budget.
insights.speaker: Mark Galeotti
insights.so_what: European elections in the next 12-18 months are a concrete political-risk calendar for Ukraine-aid continuity and should be tracked alongside battlefield developments.

insights.claim: If France and Germany begin visibly wavering on Ukraine support, more lukewarm states such as Italy could use that shift as political cover to also pull back, creating a contagion dynamic in European burden-sharing rather than independent country-by-country decisions.
insights.speaker: Mark Galeotti
insights.so_what: European aid commitments should be modeled as correlated, not independent, risks -- a wobble in one large capital could cascade quickly.

insights.claim: Ukraine's economy is effectively on life support, with Europe funding both the civilian side of the Ukrainian government and a large share of its defense expenditure; Galeotti says it is very hard to judge what would happen if that external assistance were withdrawn, but "it certainly wouldn't be pretty."
insights.speaker: Mark Galeotti
insights.so_what: Ukraine's macro stability is essentially a European fiscal-transfer story now, making continued EU budget commitments a more important variable than Ukraine's own economic fundamentals.
insights.quote: it certainly would wouldn't be pretty.

insights.claim: Amid an otherwise externally propped-up Ukrainian economy, the domestically developed drone and missile manufacturing sector stands out as a genuinely dynamic and successful part of the economy.
insights.speaker: Mark Galeotti
insights.so_what: Ukraine's indigenous defense-tech manufacturing base is the closest thing to a self-sustaining growth sector in its economy and a candidate for post-war export or investment interest.

insights.claim: Zelensky's (Zelensky's) public role functions as much as a "cheerleader" persuading the West to sustain support as it does wartime command -- Ukraine's deep-strike campaign into Russia was partly designed to convince Trump and European leaders that Ukraine was resurgent and therefore worth continued backing.
insights.speaker: Mark Galeotti
insights.so_what: Battlefield operations should partly be read as signaling moves aimed at Western capitals, not purely military tactics -- relevant to interpreting the timing of future strike campaigns.
insights.quote: Zalinsk's job is not just simply to be a war leader but in many ways also to be a cheerleader.

insights.claim: The concurrent Gulf conflict has crowded Ukraine off Western front pages, reducing the news salience of events like drone strikes on schools that previously drove public outrage, a structural risk to the durability of Western public support as the war drags on.
insights.speaker: Mark Galeotti
insights.so_what: Declining media salience is a slow-moving but real threat to Western political willingness to keep funding Ukraine, independent of battlefield conditions.
insights.quote: another drone hitting a school or whatever which once upon a time would have been front page news and keep people engaged and outraged now was relegated to two columnies on page seven

insights.claim: Galeotti argues there is no coherent US "Russia strategy" at present, only an approach to managing the Ukraine war that minimizes cost and demands on Washington while outsourcing responsibility to Europe.
insights.speaker: Mark Galeotti
insights.so_what: Investors should not expect a coordinated, durable US Russia policy framework -- current posture is reactive and cost-minimizing, meaning it can shift abruptly.
insights.quote: the honest answer is there isn't a Russia strategy. There is a Ukraine war strategy which for many is one and the same.

insights.claim: Trump initially believed he could personally and quickly resolve the war, seeking credit for succeeding where prior Democratic administrations failed, which shaped the combative Oval Office confrontation with Zelensky (Zelensky) as an apparent attempt to bully Ukraine into an unfavorable settlement with Russia.
insights.speaker: Mark Galeotti
insights.so_what: Early-term Trump negotiating tactics toward Ukraine were driven by a desire for a quick personal win, a pattern that could recur around other unresolved conflicts.

insights.claim: The bullying strategy toward Kyiv failed because Ukraine refused to accept an unfavorable deal, the Europeans backed Ukraine rather than pressuring it to concede, and Ukraine retained negotiating leverage -- leaving the White House now treating the war as a "geopolitical inconvenience" rather than a problem it can solve.
insights.speaker: Mark Galeotti
insights.so_what: With no US route to a quick deal, the war is likely to stay a slow-burn, Europe-financed conflict rather than resolve on any near-term Washington timetable.
insights.quote: in some ways it's become in many ways I would say a geopolitical inconvenience.

insights.claim: Trump reportedly holds what Galeotti calls a "19th-century notion of the world" built around great-power spheres of influence -- a mental model he shares with Putin, which helps explain why the two leaders can relate to each other despite the war, and under which Trump treats Europe as falling within America's own sphere.
insights.speaker: Mark Galeotti
insights.so_what: A shared great-power worldview between Trump and Putin is a structural reason why US-Russia rapprochement attempts keep recurring regardless of battlefield facts.
insights.quote: he has this very frankly 19th century notion of the world which is something that he shares with Putin

insights.claim: Trump's documented preference for dealing with "strong men" leaders is, in Galeotti's view, part of what allowed Zelensky (Zelensky) to later win Trump over despite their earlier Oval Office clash.
insights.speaker: Mark Galeotti
insights.so_what: Personal chemistry and image projection with Trump can move US policy toward Kyiv or Moscow more than formal strategy documents -- a soft but real variable to track.

insights.claim: US antagonism toward Europe reflects both a long-term structural pivot away from treating Europe as central to US strategy, with attention shifting toward Asia and, in practice, the Middle East, and Trump's personal grievance that Europe has freeloaded on US security guarantees while criticizing his administration.
insights.speaker: Mark Galeotti
insights.so_what: The US pivot away from Europe predates Trump and is likely to persist under future administrations, meaning European defense self-sufficiency is a durable multi-year investment theme, not a one-term anomaly.
insights.quote: America is pivoting towards Asia

insights.claim: JD Vance's confrontational February speech at the Munich Security Conference, which took Europeans to task over perceived failures on values and security, functioned as the shock event that pushed European capitals through a grief-like arc toward taking their own defense more seriously within the span of a single weekend.
insights.speaker: Mark Galeotti
insights.so_what: A single high-profile speech materially accelerated European defense-spending commitments -- a reminder that political shocks, not just budget cycles, drive European rearmament timing.
insights.quote: it was a fascinating case study in European responses that almost went through that kind of classic arc of grief

insights.claim: Despite being generally critical of the administration's approach, Galeotti personally believes the Trump administration's confrontational tactics toward Europe were probably a necessary shock to force European governments to increase their own defense burden-sharing.
insights.speaker: Mark Galeotti
insights.so_what: A credible Russia analyst conceding that confrontation "worked" on Europe is a data point suggesting the European rearmament trend is durable rather than reversible if US tone softens.
insights.quote: I wish I could disagree to be brutally honest, but I think it did take something particularly shocking.

insights.claim: Putin should be understood as a rational actor rather than a "lunatic" or purely ideological figure -- his decisions are shaped by incomplete or inaccurate information, personal prejudices, and immediate needs rather than a coherent grand strategic vision.
insights.speaker: Mark Galeotti
insights.so_what: Scenario planning on Russia should model Putin as responsive to incentives and information quality, not as an unpredictable or purely irrational actor.
insights.quote: he is a rational actor however like all rational actors his decisions will be shaped by often incomplete or inaccurate information

insights.claim: Putin's core motivations, in Galeotti's assessment, are his own personal survival, his political survival, and the ease and comfort of his personal life -- not ideology or nation-building; he is not a workaholic, rises late, and rarely travels because he faces no real electoral accountability.
insights.speaker: Mark Galeotti
insights.so_what: Any negotiated end to the war has to be evaluated first against whether it secures Putin's personal and political survival, not against what looks like a rational national outcome for Russia.
insights.quote: Putin cares about Vladimir Putin and his own actual survival, his political survival and cut the ease of his life.

insights.claim: Insecurity is described as Putin's single most fundamental character trait, traced to his childhood running with street gangs amid the ruins of postwar Leningrad, and to his decision to join the KGB not out of ideological conviction but because it was "the biggest gang in town."
insights.speaker: Mark Galeotti
insights.so_what: A psychology rooted in insecurity implies Putin will prioritize avoiding any appearance of weakness over economically rational off-ramps -- a key filter for judging which settlement terms he could actually accept.
insights.quote: He joined the KGB not because he wanted to be sword and shield of the communist party but because it seemed to be the biggest gang in town.

insights.claim: Putin launched the February 2022 invasion believing it would be a quick, easy operation -- a major miscalculation that, with hindsight into what his own security agencies reportedly told him beforehand, is now more explicable even though it was clearly wrong; he remains focused on how to survive the resulting prolonged entrapment.
insights.speaker: Mark Galeotti
insights.so_what: Putin's original war aims were built on faulty intelligence, meaning current Russian objectives are likely improvised survival goals rather than a fixed original plan -- important context for reading any negotiating position.

insights.claim: Putin avoids making difficult decisions and is currently letting the war run "almost on autopilot" rather than decisively choosing between the escalation camp and the end-the-war camp within Russian elite and public opinion, though Galeotti expects he may eventually be forced off the fence.
insights.speaker: Mark Galeotti
insights.so_what: Absent an external shock, the war is more likely to continue by inertia than end by deliberate Kremlin decision -- lowering the probability of a near-term negotiated settlement.
insights.quote: at the moment I think he's just getting away letting the war run on almost on autopilot.

insights.claim: 2026 marked a notable shift in which internal Russian elite debate over whether to end or escalate the war became publicly visible for the first time, in newspapers, blogs, and the State Duma, which Galeotti says could only happen with Putin's tacit approval, letting him later frame any eventual decision as bowing to elite consensus and shift blame if it goes wrong.
insights.speaker: Mark Galeotti
insights.so_what: Public elite debate in Russian media/parliament is a new, trackable leading indicator of where Kremlin decision-making on the war may be heading.
insights.quote: He will pitch it as the benevolent zar agreeing to this group of his aristocrats which also means that basically he can blame them if it goes wrong.

insights.claim: Putin receives three separate briefing books each morning -- from the Federal Security Service on domestic affairs, the foreign intelligence service on world events, and the Federal Protection Service on internal elite politics -- which pre-shape his assumptions about each day before any human adviser briefs him.
insights.speaker: Mark Galeotti
insights.so_what: Putin's information environment is institutionally siloed and curated, which should temper expectations that outside diplomatic messaging easily reaches or changes his views.

themes.theme: Putin's Power Structure and Succession Risk

insights.claim: Officials such as Putin's prime minister, Mishustin, function as mere "staff" rather than genuine confidants -- Galeotti describes Mishustin as "basically the head butler of the Putin country estate," whose job is to make the system run smoothly for its owner rather than to shape decisions.
insights.speaker: Mark Galeotti
insights.so_what: Formal Russian government titles are a poor guide to actual influence over Putin -- analysts and negotiators should look past the cabinet to the informal trust circle.
insights.quote: Prime Minister Mishustin is basically the head butler of the Putin country estate.

insights.claim: Putin's genuine trusted circle consists of old friends from his KGB, Leningrad, and 1990s St. Petersburg city-administration days -- mostly extremely wealthy figures outside formal government who grew rich through handed-out state corporations and sweetheart contracts, and who view Putin as their protector and meal ticket.
insights.speaker: Mark Galeotti
insights.so_what: Sanctions and diplomatic pressure aimed at this informal wealthy inner circle, rather than at formal state institutions, may be the more effective lever for influencing Putin's actual decision-making.
insights.quote: He is their protector, their krisha, their roof in Russian parliament, and he's their meal ticket.

insights.claim: In 2008, when Putin stepped back to become prime minister to work around term limits and reportedly considered not returning to the presidency, it was this wealthy inner circle -- for whom his political departure was existentially terrifying -- that was a key factor in convincing him to come back, illustrating how dependent Putin's continuity in power is on this group's financial interests.
insights.speaker: Mark Galeotti
insights.so_what: Historical precedent shows Putin's inner circle has actively intervened to keep him in power when he wavered -- a factor to weight heavily in any succession or retirement scenario analysis.

insights.claim: Because Putin's inner circle is financially dependent on his continued rule rather than composed of independent professionals, he operates inside a structural "echo chamber" that is biased toward telling him what he wants to hear rather than what he needs to hear.
insights.speaker: Mark Galeotti
insights.so_what: Expect continued strategic misjudgments from the Kremlin driven by filtered information, not just deliberate deception from adversaries -- a structural, persistent risk factor rather than a one-off error.
insights.quote: you end up with Putin in this echo chamber of people who are more likely to tell him what he wants to hear rather than what he needs to hear.

insights.claim: Dmitri Kazak, Putin's former lead negotiator with Ukraine, was frozen out and ultimately left the presidential administration after standing up to Putin -- a concrete example of how dissent is punished within Putin's inner circle.
insights.speaker: Mark Galeotti
insights.so_what: Named departures like Kazak's are a useful tell for identifying which policy positions (e.g., negotiated concessions) have fallen out of favor inside the Kremlin.
insights.quote: Kazak himself left the presidential administration clearly thinking

themes.theme: Russia Sanctions and Business Re-Entry Signal

insights.claim: Corporate advisory demand tied to Russia, which collapsed after 2022 sanctions when Galeotti's own consultancy's work mostly shrank to advising companies on how to exit, has been ticking back up over the past year as some Western companies that fled the Russian market begin quietly scoping out the possibility of an eventual return -- even though, in Galeotti's words, "they're not there yet."
insights.speaker: Mark Galeotti
insights.so_what: An early, soft signal -- not yet actionable -- that some Western corporates are quietly repositioning for a potential post-sanctions Russia market; worth tracking alongside any actual sanctions-relief developments before treating it as investable.
insights.quote: They're not there yet. They're just beginning to think it may be something that is closer to the horizon than they thought.

insights.claim: Galeotti notes he personally advised numerous companies on how to exit the Russian market after 2022, indicating sanctions/exit advisory was itself a substantial cottage industry for Russia-focused consultancies in the years immediately following the invasion.
insights.speaker: Mark Galeotti
insights.so_what: Useful baseline for distinguishing legacy exit-advisory work from genuinely new re-entry positioning when assessing how much Western corporate interest in Russia has actually shifted.
insights.quote: I did my fair share of advising companies on how they could leave Russia
